newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Split Austria govt hopes to end crisis Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Split Austria govt hopes to end crisis Saturday.

text.p: Austria's bickering government parties hope to settle a row over the privatisation of a big bank at an emergency meeting on Saturday and end a crisis which has split the coalition.
Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said on Friday he saw no danger of his one-year-old government collapsing over the imminent privatisation of Creditanstalt-Bankverein.
"Nobody, including the People's Party is seriously questioning the coalition," said Vranitzky, Europe's longest-serving government leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
The conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel fiercely opposes the sale of Creditanstalt to rival Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrats.
People's Party chief whip Andreas Khol diagnosed the coalition as suffering from a "serious illness" and a crisis of confidence but he was sure it would pull through.
"It's a serious illness, a crisis of trust...but we do not see the government collapsing. There will be no early elections," he told Reuters.

He said Creditanstalt should not be sold to a bidder just because it was prepared to pay the most money but national interests should also be considered -- a point that would be made at Saturday's meeting.
But his party was likely to receive short shrift from Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima who has made clear he is bound by European Union law to sell the bank to the highest bidder.

Khol also shrugged off concerns by Vranitzky's party over a series of talks the conservatives have had with Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party ahead of a special session of parliament next Tuesday on the privatisation.
Haider, eager to exploit the government split, has said the Freedom Party has found common ground on a number of points with the People's Party over the bank sale.

Together the People's Party and the far right could command a majority in parliament and, if pushed, Schuessel could try to embarrass Vranitzky by outvoting the Social Democrats -- a move which could seriously harm the coalition.
The Creditanstalt sell-off, seven years in the making, has developed into more than just a straight privatisation.
The bank sale has exposed a serious behind-the-scenes power struggle between the two big parties which have ruled Austria alone or together since the end of World War Two.

Creditanstalt, bankers to the Habsburg emperors during its 141-year history, is still regarded as a conservative fiefdom. The People's Party wants it to be sold to an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.

Bank Austria is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna and its acquisition of Creditanstalt would mark a symbolic blow to the conservatives, who fear Vranitzky's party is trying to consolidate its hold over Austria's overcrowded banking industry.
Creditanstalt's nearly 8,000 employees, many of whom are likely to be conservative voters, fear big job losses if Bank Austria takes over the bank.
